item.title: $2.9b P2P mobile transfers | Fijians embrace digital financial services
item.description: WHILE mobile wallets have been in existence in Fiji sine 2010, it has been revealed that person-to-person transfers have skyrocketed since 2020 with 57 million transactions totaling $2.9 billion last year. This was revealed by Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF) governor Ariff Ali at the launch of BSP Bank’s mobile wallet eDollar in Suva yesterday, who said they expected this exponential growth to continue
item.content:encoded:
WHILE mobile wallets have been in existence in Fiji sine 2010, it has been revealed that person-to-person transfers have skyrocketed since 2020 with 57 million transactions totaling $2.9 billion last year.

This was revealed by Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF) governor Ariff Ali at the launch of BSP Bank’s mobile wallet eDollar in Suva yesterday, who said they expected this exponential growth to continue based on the trend so far this year.

Similarly, Mr Ali said bank-to-wallet and wallet-to-bank transfers had also surged, while inward remittances via mobile networks now accounted for more than half of the $1.3b in annual inflows recorded last year.

He said the value of personal wallets to businesses using QR codes had also increased by almost 700 per cent in the past five years – from $86m in 2021 to $672m in 2025.

He said the number of transactions increased almost tenfold from 1.6m to 15.4m in the same period.

He added that data for the first half of 2026 revealed that QR code payments had increased by more than 44 per cent in both value and numbers over the corresponding period last year.

“For internet banking, both the value and volume have risen more than tenfold since 2015,” Mr Ali said.

“These trends clearly demonstrate that Fijians are embracing digital financial services and are ready for the next generation of payment solutions.”

Mr Ali cited the Financial Services Demand Survey Report 2025 – launched last week – that highlighted increasing digital readiness, greater mobile phone ownership, stronger demand for convenient financial services and growing consumer confidence in using digital financial products.

“The survey results revealed a significant increase in the uptake of digital channels among Fijian households, with mobile money account ownership increasing from 17 per cent in 2020 to 67 per cent in 2025.”

Mr Ali said on average, 41 per cent of banked Fijians reported having access to internet banking, representing a 30-percentage point increase from 2020.

He said the results also showed that 73 per cent of banked Fijians also owned a mobile money account.

“This tells us that customers are not necessarily choosing between banks and digital wallets. Many are using both.

“These findings confirm that the market is ready for innovations such as today’s e-wallet and that this launch comes at exactly the perfect time.”

item.title: Fiji launches first commercial bank-backed electronic wallet
item.description: BANK South Pacific (BSP) Fiji yesterday became the first commercial bank in the country to launch a bank-backed electronic wallet that marks an important milestone for banking in Fiji. Called eDollar, the digital platform is anticipated to bring the reach of Fiji’s largest banking network directly to its customers through their mobile phones, allowing for greater choice, control and convenience in
item.content:encoded:
BANK South Pacific (BSP) Fiji yesterday became the first commercial bank in the country to launch a bank-backed electronic wallet that marks an important milestone for banking in Fiji.

Called eDollar, the digital platform is anticipated to bring the reach of Fiji’s largest banking network directly to its customers through their mobile phones, allowing for greater choice, control and convenience in how they manage and move their money.

BSP Fiji relieving country head Maikash Ali said through the app, customers could create and manage up to five eWallets, each with its own unique account number and the option of domestic or international access.

“They can move funds between their BSP accounts and eWallets, transfer funds to other BSP customers, and transact across participating banks and mobile wallets,” Mr Ali said at the launch held at the Holiday Inn.

A standout feature is the QR payments allowing customers to generate their own QR code for each eWallet, enabling instant transfers between individuals and instant payments at any BSP QR merchant location.

“As banking becomes more digital, we are committed to ensuring no customer left behind. BSP eDollar empowers our valued customers with greater access to manage their own accounts, more flexibility in how they move funds plus the ability to pay by other people or businesses via QR code.”

Reserve Bank of Fiji (RBF) governor Ariff Ali said the launch marked a landmark achievement for the bank and Fiji’s financial sector, and the country’s digital transformation journey.

He said the launch was closely aligned to the central bank’s payment system modernisation agenda that sought to build a payment system that was safe, efficient, inclusive and resilient.

“In an increasingly digital and interconnected world, the ability to send and receive funds instantly is not a luxury, it has become a necessity,” Mr Ali said.

“Hence, modern payment infrastructure is no longer simply a convenience, it is the cornerstone of the financial sector and an essential component of economic development.”

item.title: Calling $8 living wage unsustainable condemns workers to poverty – FTUC
item.description: Fiji Trades Union Congress National Secretary Felix Anthony has criticised Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s comments on the proposed living wage, saying declaring it unsustainable risks condemning workers and their families to continued poverty. In a statement titled Wake Up Call , Anthony said the Prime Minister’s comments were “most unfortunate” and accused the Government of failing to adequatel
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Trades Union Congress National Secretary Felix Anthony has criticised Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka’s comments on the proposed living wage, saying declaring it unsustainable risks condemning workers and their families to continued poverty.

In a statement titled Wake Up Call , Anthony said the Prime Minister’s comments were “most unfortunate” and accused the Government of failing to adequately consider the difficulties faced by low-paid workers.

“To say that a Living Wage is unsustainable is to condemn workers to perpetual poverty,” Anthony said.

“It appears that the Prime Minister is either confused or has not paid attention to the plight of workers and their families.”

Anthony acknowledged that immediately increasing wages to $8 an hour may be difficult for some small and medium-sized businesses.

However, he argued that larger businesses were in a stronger position to absorb higher wages.

“The FTUC understands that an immediate increase to $8 may not be possible for small and medium employers. It sure is possible for big employers,” Anthony said.

He questioned claims that major companies and industries could not afford the proposed rate, accusing larger employers of using the circumstances of smaller businesses to resist wage increases.

“We have here in Fiji an excellent example of how the ‘big boys’ hide behind the ‘small boys’ and claim unsustainability,” he said.

“They threaten business closures and job losses. That’s how it’s always been.”

Anthony also linked low wages to Fiji’s continuing loss of skilled workers overseas.

“The main reason why our skilled workers are leaving our shores is low wage. People want a better life,” he said.

He compared Fiji’s wage levels with New Zealand and Australia, while acknowledging that living costs were higher in those countries.

Anthony said workers struggling financially could not be expected to deliver greater productivity.

“Workers who live in poverty and struggle to put food on the table for their families will not be productive,” he said.

“Families have had to survive on cassava and tea or rice and tea and that is the reality.”

Anthony also rejected reliance on economic growth eventually improving workers’ livelihoods.

“Here in Fiji, it’s all about business. They need to grow and hopefully workers will be better off,” he said.

“Trickle-down economics has not worked and will not. We can see that after decades of the same policy.”

Anthony also responded to the Fiji Commerce and Employers Federation’s reference to a 115 per cent increase in the National Minimum Wage over the past 20 years.

He said percentage increases meant little if workers still did not earn enough to maintain a decent standard of living.

“Workers need dollars and not percentages for a decent living,” Anthony said.

He accused the Government of responding quickly when businesses sought assistance while subjecting improvements for workers to lengthy studies and consultation processes.

“The FTUC cannot comprehend the insensitivity of Government and employers when it comes to poor workers,” he said.

Anthony called on the Government to establish a pathway towards implementing a living wage, rather than requiring an immediate $8 rate across every business.

“We call on Government to decide on a plan to implement a Living Wage within a reasonable period of time for small and medium enterprises,” he said.

He said Fiji’s commitments to decent work and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals needed to be backed by action.

“Fair wage and Decent Work are commitments that need to be implemented,” Anthony said.

He also urged workers to pay attention to the debate and described the issue as a “wake up” call.

item.title: Thrill ride provider set sights on new attractions
item.description: WITH the festival and carnival in full swing, one of the country’s biggest thrill ride service providers, Magic Land Rides, has set its sights on offering new amusement park attractions at this year’s Hibiscus Festival in Suva. Magic Land Rides Fiji director Neha Prasad said with the festival celebrating its 70th anniversary, the company planned to introduce new rides for carnival goers.
item.content:encoded:
WITH the festival and carnival in full swing, one of the country’s biggest thrill ride service providers, Magic Land Rides, has set its sights on offering new amusement park attractions at this year’s Hibiscus Festival in Suva.

Magic Land Rides Fiji director Neha Prasad said with the festival celebrating its 70th anniversary, the company planned to introduce new rides for carnival goers.

“We are not only going to introduce Energy Claw in the Hibiscus, but we will also include our Octopus, Interstellar, Rok-O-Plane, Spacekraft and Bee Ride for everyone to experience,” Ms Prasad said.

Alongside business partner Fazrat Ali, she said they operated and managed an inventory of more than 50 rides, bouncy castles, and stalls with safety at the core of the business.

“Our high-thrill rides undergo daily component checks, mandatory structural load test, and triennial non-destructive testing (NDT).

“These tests are essential to pass by the OHS covering the layout, designs, ground conditions, and mechanical integrity before receiving operational certification, which we possess for all our rides.

“Our maintenance routine ensures checks on safety devices, drives and restraints and routine component testing of bolts, lock pins and transmissions and a structural load testing is conducted prior to public operation.”

She explained their jobs at various festivals across the country had also opened the door for employment and on the job training for Fijians.

“We provide on-the-job skill training for temporary workers in safety and customer service. We also partner with other local vendors who also have rides and other attractions, food stands, crafters, and retail vendors along with increasing sales for regional suppliers and adjacent storefronts during peak hours.”

With the Hibiscus Festival more than two weeks away, Ms Prasad said they hoped to gain a wider network and attention towards a long-term goal of establishing an amusement park.

item.title: Journey beyond the Hibiscus Queen crown
item.description: Seventy years ago, the role of women in Fiji and around the world looked very different. But one thing has remained remarkably consistent through seven decades of the Hibiscus Festival — the opportunity it gives young women to discover themselves, find their voices and step into the wider world with greater confidence.
item.content:encoded:
Seventy years ago, the role of women in Fiji and around the world looked very different.

But one thing has remained remarkably consistent through seven decades of the Hibiscus Festival — the opportunity it gives young women to discover themselves, find their voices and step into the wider world with greater confidence.

Since the first festival in 1956, thousands of young Fijian women have taken the stage at Hibiscus.

Only one contestant each year walks away with the crown, but many former queens and contestants say the real rewards have lasted far beyond the week of festivities.

For the 2026 FMF Hibiscus Festival director Ellen Whippy-Knight, reconnecting with former contestants has offered a glimpse into the lasting influence of the festival.

“In reconnecting with so many former queens and contestants, it is heartwarming to learn how their lives were enriched by their festival experience,” she said.

“Self-belief, time management, goal setting and confidence in public are recurring themes of what these women took from the competition.”

The stories of former contestants reflect the changing face of Fijian society itself.

From its colonial beginnings, through decades of social and political change, the rise of feminism and the increasing education and participation of women in public life, Hibiscus has provided a platform for young women from different backgrounds to be seen and heard.

They have come from villages and towns, entered the workforce, built businesses, advocated for causes, raised families and contributed to their communities in ways that previous generations of women may never have imagined.

And the lessons learned under the Hibiscus spotlight have often remained long after the crown was passed on.

Laurie Crowe, the 1961 winner, remembers her experience as something deeply special.

“It was a very special experience for me at the time and one I am grateful for,” she reflected.

“I wish I’d known then what I know now.”

For 1974 contestant Karen McAllister, the experience was initially unfamiliar.

“As a young, white, unworldly Fijian, being invited to take part in a beauty contest was flattering but also bewildering,” she recalled.

With the benefit of hindsight, however, she came to see the experience differently.

“What initially seemed like a strange and confusing experience became a valuable lesson in confidence, resilience and keeping a broader perspective on society and the world.”

That same year, winner Sandra Hazleman discovered a confidence that would influence the woman she became.

“The festival shaped the woman I became. It gave me confidence, strengthened my public speaking abilities and inspired a life-long passion to help others,” she said.

For 1982 winner Lorna Christoferson, Hibiscus became the catalyst for stepping into business at a young age.

“Having the opportunity to meet and interact with many great people gave me the confidence to start my own business,” she said.

The festival also taught her an important lesson about authenticity and conviction.

“You must believe 100 per cent in whatever you choose to speak about because if you’re unsure you will come across badly.”

For Shital Ram, the 2002 winner, Hibiscus provided something equally important — a sense of belonging.

“Being a part of the Hibiscus festival brought me so much support and made me feel like I truly belonged,” she said.

She still remembers the warmth she received whenever she introduced herself as the “Marama ni Wainibokasi”.

Nearly a decade later, 2011 winner Alisi Rabukawaqa took a different lesson from the experience — learning to manage her time and energy while using her platform to advocate for the protection of Fiji’s oceans and land.

The festival, in that sense, has evolved alongside the women who participate in it.

What may once have been primarily viewed as a beauty competition has become a platform for young women to develop confidence, leadership skills and a public voice.

item.title: Sydney lawyer with Fiji links arrested in Australia
item.description: A Sydney lawyer with Fijian roots and reported links to the notorious Alameddine crime family has been charged over an alleged armed kidnapping and home invasion in Sydney’s western suburbs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald . The newspaper reports that 27-year-old Sylvan Singh, a former solicitor at his father’s Parramatta-based Redline Legal, was arrested at his Ryde home on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
A Sydney lawyer with Fijian roots and reported links to the notorious Alameddine crime family has been charged over an alleged armed kidnapping and home invasion in Sydney’s western suburbs, according to the Sydney Morning Herald .

The newspaper reports that 27-year-old Sylvan Singh, a former solicitor at his father’s Parramatta-based Redline Legal, was arrested at his Ryde home on Tuesday.

Singh has been charged with allegedly directing a kidnapping carried out by a group armed with machetes and baseball bats at Pemulwuy last year.

According to the report, three masked men allegedly blocked a ute carrying the intended victim before forcing the man into a stolen Mercedes.

The alleged victim managed to escape when the Mercedes stopped a short time later, prompting the group to flee into nearby bushland.

Singh is also accused of orchestrating a home invasion at an Ermington property in February 2025, about two weeks after the alleged kidnapping.

Four people allegedly entered the home, stole several electronic devices and assaulted a 17-year-old boy and a 48-year-old man.

The Sydney Morning Herald reports Singh was charged at Gladesville Police Station and was due to appear before Burwood Local Court on Wednesday.

The two alleged incidents have been investigated under Strike Force Velinda, which the newspaper reports has resulted in 10 charges.

Singh was himself the victim of a separate gangland shooting in May last year.

He was travelling in a Toyota Hilux with underworld figure Dawood Zakaria when the vehicle came under attack.

Zakaria was fatally shot, while Singh survived after suffering gunshot wounds to his arm and shoulder.

According to the report, the shooting was linked to tensions surrounding the defection of a senior Alameddine member to a rival crime syndicate and led NSW Police to establish Taskforce Falcon in response to escalating gangland violence.

Several people have since been charged with Zakaria’s murder and the attempted murder of Singh.

The newspaper also reports that Singh’s practising certificate was suspended by the Council of the Law Society of NSW in September.

The allegations against Singh remain before the courts and have not been proven.

item.title: Appeal allowed over evidence gaps
item.description: THE Court of Appeal has granted leave to appeal to a man convicted of raping his 15-year-old daughter, after finding that the trial judge may not have properly considered all the evidence presented during the trial. The 45-year-old was convicted by the High Court on a count of rape and sentenced in 2024 to 12 years, 11 months, and 23 days imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 10 years, 11 mont
item.content:encoded:
THE Court of Appeal has granted leave to appeal to a man convicted of raping his 15-year-old daughter, after finding that the trial judge may not have properly considered all the evidence presented during the trial.

The 45-year-old was convicted by the High Court on a count of rape and sentenced in 2024 to 12 years, 11 months, and 23 days imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 10 years, 11 months, and 23 days.

In a ruling delivered late last month, Court of Appeal president Justice Isikeli Mataitoga granted leave for the appeal to proceed after finding the appellant had reasonable prospects of success.

The appeal against conviction was based on two grounds — that the evidence did not support the conviction, and that the trial judge failed to properly consider the delayed reporting of the alleged offence.

Through his lawyer, the man argued that the evidence at trial raised questions about who was responsible for the complainant’s pregnancy.

The Appeals Court noted that the complainant had given evidence that both her father and uncle had sexually assaulted her around the same period.

Justice Mataitoga said the trial judge had only considered the man’s involvement and did not adequately address the evidence relating to the uncle.

The complainant had told the court that the alleged rape by her father occurred in late May 2020, while she had also identified her uncle as another person who had allegedly engaged in sexual activity with her.

On the issue of delayed reporting, the court also found the appeal ground had merit because the victim only reported the alleged rape after the birth of her child, and the circumstances surrounding the delay required further consideration.

“I am satisfied that the failure to make the report of the rape by the complainant until her child is born is a serious failure in terms of the veracity of the evidence she has given in this trial,” he said.
